title: Competitive inhibition of the Nipah virus matrix protein by conivaptan: from binding pocket dynamics to protein-membrane interactions.
abstract: The recurrent outbreaks of Nipah virus since its first emergence have intensified efforts to identify effective antiviral therapeutics. The matrix protein is a key structural protein that maintains virion architecture and plays a crucial role in anchoring the virus to the host plasma membrane. Binding of phosphatidylinositol-4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2) to the matrix protein promotes conformational changes that facilitate membrane association and initiate viral assembly. Therefore, an effective small-molecule inhibitor should not only compete with PIP2 for binding to the Nipah virus matrix protein (NiVM) but also disrupt its interaction with the host membrane. Using virtual screening of FDA-approved drugs combined with ensemble docking, we identified conivaptan as a potential inhibitor of the Nipah virus matrix protein. The multivalent interactions of conivaptan establish stable binding within the PIP2-binding pocket while simultaneously rewiring protein-membrane interactions. In the presence of PIP2, NiVM anchors to the membrane through multiple charged residues, resulting in pronounced local bilayer deformation, an early signature of membrane remodeling. In contrast, conivaptan binding weakens membrane anchoring and preserves a more ordered and compact bilayer, thereby suppressing membrane deformation. Together, these findings identify conivaptan as a promising repurposable inhibitor of the Nipah virus matrix protein and provide a mechanistic framework for targeting virus-membrane interactions during viral assembly.

title_zh: conivaptan 对 尼帕病毒 基质蛋白的竞争性抑制:从结合袋动力学到蛋白质-膜相互作用。
source_body_en: The recurrent outbreaks of Nipah virus since its first emergence have intensified efforts to identify effective antiviral therapeutics. The matrix protein is a key structural protein that maintains virion architecture and plays a crucial role in anchoring the virus to the host plasma membrane. Binding of phosphatidylinositol-4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2) to the matrix protein promotes conformational changes that facilitate membrane association and initiate viral assembly. Therefore, an effective small-molecule inhibitor should not only compete with PIP2 for binding to the Nipah virus matrix protein (NiVM) but also disrupt its interaction with the host membrane. Using virtual screening of FDA-approved drugs combined with ensemble docking, we identified conivaptan as a potential inhibitor of the Nipah virus matrix protein. The multivalent interactions of conivaptan establish stable binding within the PIP2-binding pocket while simultaneously rewiring protein-membrane interactions. In the presence of PIP2, NiVM anchors to the membrane through multiple charged residues, resulting in pronounced local bilayer deformation, an early signature of membrane remodeling. In contrast, conivaptan binding weakens membrane anchoring and preserves a more ordered and compact bilayer, thereby suppressing membrane deformation. Together, these findings identify conivaptan as a promising repurposable inhibitor of the Nipah virus matrix protein and provide a mechanistic framework for targeting virus-membrane interactions during viral assembly.

title: CRISPR/Cas13a-Based Nucleic Acid-Functionalized Discrete Floating-Gate Field-Effect Transistor for Amplification-Free Rapid Nipah Virus Detection.
abstract: Nipah virus (NiV) is a highly lethal zoonotic pathogen, and existing rapid diagnostic tools are scarce and reliant on nucleic acid amplification. In this study, we designed and fabricated a thin-film field-effect transistor with an IGZO channel and, for the first time, combined a discrete AuNP floating gate with the CRISPR/Cas13a system to achieve amplification-free detection of NiV. A pair of partially complementary nucleic acid reporter probes was used to attach AuNPs onto the channel, forming a nucleic acid-functionalized discrete floating gate. Under positive gate voltage, the AuNPs electrostatically induce mirror charges in the IGZO channel, amplifying the sensing signal. Additionally, the electrons can be injected from AuNPs into the channel via the Fowler-Nordheim tunneling effect under negative gate voltage, as a potential complementary sensing mechanism. The AuNPs are immobilized via nucleic acid strands, ensuring good biocompatibility. CrRNA was designed and the CRISPR system was optimized for compatibility with the FET, achieving amplification-free detection of NiV standards down to 10° copies/μL within 10 min. This study not only provides a reliable and rapid detection tool for NiV but also establishes a biosensing framework applicable to other pathogens.

title: Self-Amplifying RNA Vaccines After the First Approvals: Technology, Development Landscape, and Regulatory Science Considerations
abstract: Self-amplifying RNA (saRNA) is a next-generation nucleic acid vaccine platform that enhances antigen expression through intracellular amplification of replicon RNA without producing infectious virions. saRNA constructs encode an alphavirus-derived replicase comprising nonstructural proteins nsP1–nsP4 and can elicit robust immune responses at low RNA doses. Replication intermediates may activate RIG-I, MDA5, and endosomal TLR3/7/8, contributing adjuvant-like activity. Kostaive (ARCT-154; zapomeran) became the first saRNA vaccine to receive full marketing approval in Japan in 2023, followed by authorization in the European Union in 2025 and the United Kingdom in 2026, demonstrating the platform’s clinical and regulatory feasibility. Development now extends beyond COVID-19 to seasonal and pandemic influenza, rabies, Crimean–Congo hemorrhagic fever, Nipah virus disease, and individualized cancer vaccines. However, the longer transcripts and additional replicase and subgenomic-promoter elements make in vitro transcription efficiency, full-length RNA content, double-stranded and truncated RNA impurities, lipid nanoparticle encapsulation, and potency testing particularly important. Regulatory assessment increasingly focuses on correct replicase and antigen expression, the magnitude and duration of self-amplification, biodistribution and persistence, and comparability. This review synthesizes the scientific basis, development landscape, manufacturing challenges, and regulatory science considerations of saRNA vaccines.

title_zh: 首次批准后的自扩增 RNA 疫苗:技术、发展前景和监管科学考虑因素
source_body_en: Self-amplifying RNA (saRNA) is a next-generation nucleic acid vaccine platform that enhances antigen expression through intracellular amplification of replicon RNA without producing infectious virions. saRNA constructs encode an alphavirus-derived replicase comprising nonstructural proteins nsP1–nsP4 and can elicit robust immune responses at low RNA doses. Replication intermediates may activate RIG-I, MDA5, and endosomal TLR3/7/8, contributing adjuvant-like activity. Kostaive (ARCT-154; zapomeran) became the first saRNA vaccine to receive full marketing approval in Japan in 2023, followed by authorization in the European Union in 2025 and the United Kingdom in 2026, demonstrating the platform’s clinical and regulatory feasibility. Development now extends beyond COVID-19 to seasonal and pandemic influenza, rabies, Crimean–Congo hemorrhagic fever, Nipah virus disease, and individualized cancer vaccines. However, the longer transcripts and additional replicase and subgenomic-promoter elements make in vitro transcription efficiency, full-length RNA content, double-stranded and truncated RNA impurities, lipid nanoparticle encapsulation, and potency testing particularly important. Regulatory assessment increasingly focuses on correct replicase and antigen expression, the magnitude and duration of self-amplification, biodistribution and persistence, and comparability. This review synthesizes the scientific basis, development landscape, manufacturing challenges, and regulatory science considerations of saRNA vaccines.
